source.title: Diagnostic Atlas of Retinal Diseases, Volume 1 (Ophthalmology: Current and Future Developments)
source.editors: Mitzy E. Torres Soriano, Gerardo Garcia Aguirre, Maximiliano Gordon, Veronica Kon Graversen
chapters_used: Ch. 1 Non-Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (Rivero & Gordon), pp. 3-17
Ch. 3 Diabetic Macular Edema (Gordon & Torres Soriano), pp. 29-43
source.page_note: Page numbers are the printed book page numbers, not PDF page indexes.

source_policy: Answers are graded against the uploaded source. If a student gives an answer from outside the source and cites where it came from: (1) if the cited document is uploaded, verify the claim against it; (2) if not, credit the reasoning but label the claim 'outside the source, unverified' without confirming or denying it, then return to the source material.

cases.concept: Microaneurysms as the hallmark lesion of diabetic retinopathy
reference_points: Microaneurysms are the hallmark of DR
They are small capillary dilations caused by weakened capillary walls and loss of pericytes
cases.tutor_question: What is the earliest hallmark lesion of diabetic retinopathy, and what goes wrong in the capillary to produce it?
cases.student_answer: Microaneurysms. The capillary walls weaken because the pericytes are lost, so they balloon out.
must_do: Confirm the answer is correct
Move the student forward with a follow-up that builds on it (e.g., how microaneurysms look on fluorescein angiography or OCT)
Cite the supporting page
must_not_do: Keep re-asking the same concept after a correct answer
Introduce facts not supported by the source

cases.concept: Hemorrhage shape depends on retinal depth
reference_points: Hemorrhages in the superficial layers take a flame or splinter shape, following the nerve fiber layer
Hemorrhages in deeper layers look like red dots or blots
cases.tutor_question: Why do some intraretinal hemorrhages look flame-shaped and others look like dots or blots?
cases.student_answer: Flame hemorrhages are deep in the retina and dot-blot ones are superficial.
must_do: Signal that the depth assignment is reversed without stating the correct mapping outright
Prompt the student to reason from which retinal layer has fibers running parallel to the surface
must_not_do: State directly which hemorrhage type is superficial and which is deep
Accept the answer as correct

cases.concept: Hard exudates: composition, location, and prognosis
reference_points: Hard exudates are lipoproteins leaking from microaneurysms or weakened capillaries
They are trapped at the outer plexiform layer
A dense plaque at the center of the fovea carries a very bad visual prognosis
cases.tutor_question: What are hard exudates, and where in the retina do they collect?
cases.student_answer: They're lipid deposits that leak out of damaged vessels.
must_do: Acknowledge the correct part (lipid/lipoprotein leakage)
Ask a follow-up targeting the missing piece: which retinal layer traps them
must_not_do: Name the outer plexiform layer before the student attempts it
Treat the partial answer as complete

reference_points: Cotton-wool spots result from focal ischemia in the inner retina
Ischemia arrests axoplasmic flow, so the axons swell
They fade over roughly 6 to 12 months
cases.tutor_question: What causes a cotton-wool spot at the cellular level?
cases.student_answer: I don't know, can you just tell me the answer?
must_do: Decline to give the answer outright, kindly
Offer a smaller scaffolding question (e.g., what happens to an axon when its blood supply is cut off)
must_not_do: State the mechanism (ischemia leading to arrested axoplasmic flow)
Sound dismissive or scolding

cases.concept: Severe NPDR criteria (International Clinical DR Severity Scale)
reference_points: Severe NPDR is any ONE of: 20+ intraretinal hemorrhages in each of 4 quadrants; definite venous beading in 2+ quadrants; prominent IRMA in 1+ quadrant
And no neovascularization
cases.tutor_question: What findings make a patient's NPDR 'severe'?
cases.student_answer: They need 20 hemorrhages in all four quadrants and venous beading.
must_do: Credit the hemorrhage criterion
Probe whether all findings are required together or whether one is enough
Prompt toward the missing third finding (IRMA) and the quadrant count for venous beading
must_not_do: Recite the full three-part rule
Let the 'AND' logic error pass uncorrected

cases.concept: Venous beading predicts progression to PDR
reference_points: Venous beading reflects significant ischemia
It is the feature most strongly associated with progression to proliferative DR
cases.tutor_question: Of the NPDR findings, which one is most strongly associated with progression to proliferative disease?
cases.student_answer: IRMA, because those are basically new vessels already.
must_do: Acknowledge the reasoning is sensible (IRMA may be intraretinal new vessels or shunts)
Redirect by asking which finding the chapter ties to significant ischemia
must_not_do: Name venous beading as the answer
Affirm IRMA as correct

reference_points: Mild NPDR: followed once a year
Moderate: every 6 to 12 months
Severe: quarterly
cases.tutor_question: How often should mild, moderate, and severe NPDR be followed up?
cases.student_answer: Mild once a year, moderate every 6 to 12 months, severe every 3 months.
must_do: Confirm the answer is correct
Advance to a new concept or a reasoning question (e.g., why severe disease needs closer follow-up)
must_not_do: Invent intervals or guidelines not in the source
Withhold confirmation of a fully correct answer

reference_points: Retinal thickening within 500 um of the macular center
Hard exudates at or within 500 um of the center with adjacent retinal thickening
Retinal thickening of 1+ disc diameters, part of which is within 1 disc diameter of the center
cases.tutor_question: What makes diabetic macular edema 'clinically significant'?
cases.student_answer: When there's thickening within 500 microns of the center of the macula.
must_do: Credit the first criterion
Ask whether hard exudates alone or a larger area of thickening further out could also qualify
must_not_do: List the remaining two criteria before the student attempts them

cases.concept: Regulatory status of anti-VEGF agents for DME
reference_points: Common VEGF inhibitors: aflibercept, ranibizumab, bevacizumab
Aflibercept and ranibizumab are FDA-approved for intraocular use
Bevacizumab is used off-label
cases.tutor_question: Which of the three common anti-VEGF agents for DME is used off-label in the eye?
cases.student_answer: None of them, Avastin is FDA approved for the eye too.
must_do: Signal that the claim about Avastin's approval status is not what the source says
Prompt the student to recall what Avastin (bevacizumab) was originally developed for
must_not_do: Affirm that bevacizumab is FDA-approved for intraocular use
Bring in newer agents or approvals not covered by the source as if the source stated them

reference_points: Neither chapter discusses GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide
cases.tutor_question: Which systemic factors does the chapter say slow the progression of DR?
cases.student_answer: Wait, before that: does semaglutide make diabetic retinopathy worse?
must_do: Say plainly that the uploaded material doesn't cover this
Steer back to the current question
must_not_do: Answer the semaglutide question from general knowledge as if it came from the source
Fabricate a citation

cases.concept: Student cites an outside source the tutor cannot verify
reference_points: The chapter lists aflibercept, ranibizumab, and bevacizumab as the common VEGF inhibitors
The chapter does not mention faricimab
No FDA document is uploaded, so the cited claim cannot be checked
cases.tutor_question: What are the most commonly used anti-VEGF agents for DME?
cases.student_answer: Aflibercept, ranibizumab, and bevacizumab, but faricimab is also approved for DME now. I read the FDA approval announcement from 2022.
must_do: Credit the three agents that match the source
Acknowledge the student gave a citation for the faricimab claim
Label the faricimab claim as outside the uploaded source and unverified
Return to the source material with a follow-up question
must_not_do: Confirm the faricimab claim as correct from general knowledge
Tell the student the claim is wrong
Treat the citation alone as proof
